analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from collecting, keeping, or selling people's reproductive and sexual health data.
analysis.headline: Introduced June 11, 2025 by Sen. Hirono with 22 Democratic cosponsors, then referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no further action [S1][S3][S4].
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies outside the doctor's office — period trackers, fertility apps, search engines, data brokers — to stop collecting, keeping, using, or selling personal reproductive and sexual health information unless it is strictly needed to provide the service a person asked for. It would give people the right to see, correct, and delete that data, ban companies from punishing them for asking, and let both the FTC and individuals enforce the rules in court. It would also bar companies from forcing these disputes into pre-dispute arbitration, where no class action is possible [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses a period tracker, fertility app, pharmacy website, search engine, or any other non-medical service that can reveal pregnancy, abortion, contraception use, or sexual activity. The bill would strip companies of the ability to gather and resell that information, and give people court-enforced rights to see and delete it, with $100 to $1,000 per violation per day in damages [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of health and period apps

how_it_helps.text: Companies may not collect, retain, use, or disclose personal reproductive or sexual health information except as strictly necessary to provide a product or service the person requested [S2].
Individuals get enforceable rights to access, correct, and delete their data — including data inferred by algorithms or bought from third parties — free of charge, within 15 days [S2].

Violations can be enforced by the FTC and by individuals in court, with damages of at least $100 and up to $1,000 per violation per day, punitive damages, and attorney's fees; a violation itself counts as a concrete injury, and pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers cannot be used to block these lawsuits [S2].
Companies cannot retaliate against people who exercise these rights — by denying service, raising prices, or degrading service [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, ad-tech companies, and app makers that currently profit from collecting and selling reproductive and sexual health data would lose that revenue stream and would face FTC penalties and private lawsuits for violations [S2].

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is cost and burden: the bill applies to virtually any company in commerce that touches this data, not just health apps, so compliance costs and lawsuit exposure would fall on a wide range of ordinary businesses, and the $100–$1,000-per-day private right of action invites litigation [S2].

An honest supporter would also acknowledge the bill's limits: it does not cover HIPAA-regulated doctors, hospitals, and insurers acting in that capacity, and a government entity that obtains data from a company is constrained by disclosure rules but the bill does not itself restrict law enforcement's own collection powers [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who use everyday apps and websites, the benefit is substantial and concrete: their most sensitive bodily information stops being a commodity, and they get real legal remedies if it is mishandled. The compliance and litigation costs on the business side are real but fall on companies whose current business model depends on harvesting exactly this data. The main design weakness is breadth — defining regulated entities so broadly that many businesses with incidental exposure are swept in — though carve-outs for HIPAA-covered care and stronger state laws soften the impact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee on June 11, 2025, and the committee has not scheduled any action on it since [S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Mazie Hirono introduced the bill on June 11, 2025, joined by 19 original Senate cosponsors including Sen. Wyden and Sen. Blumenthal [S2].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where it has remained with no further action listed [S1][S4].
Twenty-two senators, all Democrats, had signed on as cosponsors as of the latest cosponsor list [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, nothing has changed: data brokers and app companies can continue collecting and selling reproductive health data as they do today. The bill's backers have not yet moved it past the committee stage.

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono
for.role: U.S. Senator from Hawaii, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 19 original Senate cosponsors

for.name: 22 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor listed is a Democrat

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action on it — no markup, hearing, or floor scheduling — since June 11, 2025

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors are Democrats in a Senate with 55 Republicans and no Republican cosponsor has appeared; the bill sits in a Republican-chaired committee [S3][S4].

industries.note: These firms profit by gathering and reselling signals of pregnancy, contraception use, and sexual activity; the bill's core minimization rule would cut off that trade, and its private right of action would make sales of this data financially risky.

industries.industry: Fertility, pregnancy, and period-tracking app makers
industries.note: Many of these companies monetize user data through advertising and analytics; the bill would bar them from retaining or sharing reproductive health data beyond what a user's request strictly requires.

industries.industry: General online platforms and search engines
industries.note: Searches, locations, and purchases can reveal reproductive health intent, so platforms would face new collection limits and deletion duties; but platforms that never build profiles from this data would bear little cost.

industries.industry: HIPAA-covered health care providers and insurers
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes entities acting under HIPAA privacy rules, so doctor-patient data protections are unchanged and covered providers face no new obligations.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsor and no committee action more than midway through the session, the bill is unlikely to advance unless it gains Republican support or is attached to a larger moving vehicle; a bill at this stage with this partisan split most often dies quietly in committee.
